title: The Harbour and the Throne
description: You are a junior interpreter attached to Raffles' expedition. In one tense week, you must help British officers and Johor leaders speak across law, trade and succession. A port may be founded, but only if the right people agree.
learningObjectives: Explain why the East India Company wanted a port at the southern end of the Straits of Malacca
Describe the disputed Johor succession and why Raffles recognised Tengku Hussein
Evaluate the risks each stakeholder took in signing the 1819 agreements

player.name: junior-interpreter
player.role: Junior interpreter attached to Raffles' expedition
player.brief: You translate, carry messages and compare what each side says. You do not command anyone, but your choices can shape who speaks, who signs and what kind of settlement begins.

sharedContext.text: British merchants want a safe harbour near the southern end of the Straits of Malacca. Raffles has come to Singapore to seek a post, but he must avoid a clash with the Dutch. The Temenggong can talk with him, yet the right to grant land belongs to the Sultan, and the Johor throne is disputed.

spans.quote: British merchants trading with China complained that they had no safe harbour of their own at the southern end of the Straits of Malacca.
he was to establish a post at the southern end of the Straits but to avoid any collision with the Dutch
only the Sultan of Johor could lawfully grant land to the Company. And the Johor throne itself was disputed.

endings.title: A Post Without a Strong Grant
endings.summary: Raffles moves too fast and treats local control as enough. The Company has a foothold, but its claim is weak because the Temenggong is not the sovereign. The opening may still happen, yet the legal basis is fragile from the start.

historicalOutcome.text: This does not match the record. The handout says the first agreement with the Temenggong had a weakness because only the Sultan could lawfully grant land. Raffles then pursued Hussein's claim and signed a wider treaty on 6 February 1819.

spans.quote: The Temenggong governed Singapore, but he was not the sovereign; only the Sultan of Johor could lawfully grant land to the Company.
On 6 February 1819 a treaty was signed between the East India Company, represented by Raffles, Sultan Hussein and Temenggong Abdul Rahman.

endings.divergence: In this ending, the expedition acts as if the preliminary agreement is enough and never secures the stronger treaty recorded in the source.
reflectionQuestions: Why was the Temenggong's signature alone a problem?
Would speed matter more than legality in a port dispute?
Who would benefit most from a weak agreement?

endings.title: The Settlement Stalls
endings.summary: You support the preliminary agreement but avoid the succession issue. Without a Sultan's lawful grant, the project slows and its future remains doubtful. Everyone has less to lose at once, but also less to gain.

historicalOutcome.text: This differs from the record. The handout says Raffles recognised Hussein and a treaty was signed on 6 February 1819, permitting a factory at Singapore.

spans.quote: Hussein arrived in Singapore in early February 1819, and Raffles recognised him as Sultan Hussein Shah of Johor.
The Company was permitted to establish a factory, or trading post, at Singapore.

endings.divergence: In this ending, the expedition stops after the 30 January agreement instead of moving to the 6 February treaty.
reflectionQuestions: Why might some people prefer a smaller, safer step?
What did Raffles gain by taking the extra risk of recognising Hussein?
How can delaying a decision also be a decision?

endings.title: The Chance Is Lost
endings.summary: Fearing dispute, you push for withdrawal. The expedition leaves without creating a post. This avoids an immediate clash, but it also gives up the chance to shape trade at the southern end of the Straits.

historicalOutcome.text: This does not match the record. The sources say Raffles had permission to look for a site, reached Singapore, and a treaty was signed on 6 February 1819 to establish a trading post.

endings.divergence: In this ending, caution defeats the expedition before the recorded treaty can happen.
reflectionQuestions: What British goal is abandoned in this ending?

endings.title: The Treaty Is Signed
endings.summary: You help the parties complete the treaty through Hussein's recognition. The Company gains a trading post, Hussein and the Temenggong gain payment and status, and Farquhar is left to run the new settlement. Dutch protest comes at once, but the port begins.

historicalOutcome.text: This matches the record in the handout. On 6 February 1819 the treaty was signed, the Company was allowed to establish a factory at Singapore, Hussein and the Temenggong received annual payments, and Farquhar became Resident and Commandant.

The Company was permitted to establish a factory, or trading post, at Singapore.
